beats.title: Don't take my word for anything here
beats.body: This room has one idea in it. You are going to *find* it yourself — by moving things and watching what happens — before I give it a name. Nothing below is to be memorised yet. Just look, drag, and notice.
What is the *direction* of a curve at a single point?
beats.aside: A straight line has one obvious slope. A curve bends — it is steeper here than there. So what could "steepness" even mean at a single point, where there is no second point to compare against? Hold the question. Don't answer it yet.

beats.body: Two points sit on this curve, joined by a straight line. Its slope is easy — rise over run. Now **drag the moving point toward the fixed one** and keep your eyes on the slope number.
beats.reveal: Did you feel it? The line stopped swinging. As the gap closed, the slope stopped changing — it *settled* on one number instead of running away.

beats.body: But look at what you just did. To get a slope you needed *two* points and the run between them. At the very end you wanted them to be the *same* point — run zero, rise zero, $0/0$, which means nothing.
beats.aside: So the honest slope needs two points, yet the direction-at-a-point wants one. That contradiction is the whole difficulty. Everything else in this room is how mathematics slips between the horns of it.

beats.body: Set the run aside for a moment and just *look* at the curve near the point. Drag the slider and zoom in. Keep going.
beats.reveal: There it is. Zoom in far enough and the curve becomes indistinguishable from a straight line. A smooth curve, up close, *is* straight — and that straight line has a single, definite slope.

beats.body: You watched the slope settle as the two points merged. Commit to an answer: as the gap shrinks all the way to nothing, that average slope —
beats.reveal: It settles on one exact number — the slope of that straight line you found by zooming. We never reach zero gap; we watch what the slope *approaches*. That word, *approaches*, is the escape from $0/0$ — and it is exactly why the previous hall had to be about limits.

beats.body: Before we name anything, test how fragile this is. Here is a curve with a sharp corner. Put the fixed point *on* the corner and drag the other point in from one side, then the other. Watch the slope.
beats.reveal: The two sides disagree — one slope from the left, a different one from the right. Nothing settles. At a corner there is no single direction, and the mathematics refuses to invent one. The idea only works where the curve is smooth — and where it fails, that failure is information.

beats.body: Put the three things together. The average slope over a shrinking step *settles* on a number. Up close the curve *is* the line with that slope. And it exists only where the curve is smooth.
beats.after: That settled number is the answer to the question you were holding. It has a name — two, in fact. The number the average slopes *approach* is a **limit**. The limit, taken here, is called the **derivative**.

beats.body: Only now, with the idea already in your hands, is the symbol worth writing. The **derivative** of $f$ at $x$ is the limit of the average slope as the step $h$ closes to nothing:
beats.label: the derivative
beats.caption: Read it aloud as what you did: shrink the step $h$, watch the average slope, take the number it approaches.

beats.body: Take $f(x) = x^2$ and follow the definition — no rules, just the limit you already understand.
steps: Expand the numerator: (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2) / h
Let h approach 0: the leftover h vanishes
beats.label: for f(x) = x²
beats.after: Every rule you will meet — power, product, quotient, chain — is this same limit, worked out once so you never expand $(x+h)^n$ by hand again.

beats.body: This is position against time. Drag the moment $t$ and read the tangent's slope. That slope is the *speed at that instant* — the speedometer reading, the thing that felt impossible at the start.
beats.aside: Differentiate position and you get velocity. The abstract slope and the everyday speedometer are the same object, seen twice.

beats.body: Here is a hill. Drag the point until the tangent lies perfectly flat. Where does that happen?
beats.aside: Exactly at the top. A maximum or minimum sits where the slope is zero — which is why every optimization problem (largest volume, least cost, shortest path) becomes the single equation $f'(x) = 0$.

beats.kicker: Before you leave — think, don't scroll
beats.body: You will remember this far better if you say it back in your own words. Nothing here is graded; it is kept only for you, and you can read it again before the exam.
prompts: Explain the derivative to your future self, in two sentences.
What surprised you in this room?
beats.draw: On paper, sketch a curve, a point on it, and the tangent there. Label the slope. Ten seconds — the drawing is the point, not its neatness.

beats.body: You arrived with a question and found its answer with your own hands. Everything in this gallery — every rule, every application, every exam question about a rate, a slope, a maximum, a velocity — is this one sentence:
beats.after: That is what to carry out of the room.
